query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Warm forging at moderate temperatures followed by a short annealing step, applied to eutectic high-entropy alloys with lamellar microstructures, will simultaneously increase both strength and ductility compared to the as-cast condition by refining the lamellar spacing.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with coarse two-phase lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing: forging at 700–900°C followed by a brief annealing at approximately 900–1000°C and rapid cooling.
generation.conditions: Applies to EHEAs displaying fine-scale lamellar microstructures after casting. The forging temperature and annealing duration should be tuned to optimize lamellar refinement without causing excessive grain growth.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar spacing and interphase boundaries induced by the thermomechanical treatment.
generation.mechanism: Reduced lamellar spacing creates additional barriers to dislocation motion, thereby increasing strength, while the refined lamellae also enhance strain accommodation and delay crack initiation, improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Expect about a 20% increase in yield strength and around 10% improvement in elongation relative to the as-cast baseline.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with relatively coarse lamellae (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the as-cast state).
generation.boundary: Effective in systems with stable refractory or intermetallic lamellar phases; overly high forging temperatures or excessive annealing times might coarsen the microstructure, reducing the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: Exact forging temperature, strain level, and annealing parameters require optimization for each EHEA composition to ensure lamellar refinement without over-aging or partial dissolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same as-cast eutectic HEA alloy. One reference set remains in the as-cast condition, while the other is subjected to forging at ~800°C followed by a short high-temperature anneal. Characterize lamellar spacing (e.g., via SEM or TEM) and measure tensile properties of both sets.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (tensile tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If forging plus short annealing does not reduce lamellar spacing or does not produce any measurable improvements in both strength and ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. chosen.lever: controlled forging plus short annealing to refine lamella spacing
chosen.technique: warm forging at moderate temperatures followed by short high-temperature annealing and rapid cooldown
chosen.conditions: eutectic high-entropy alloy with lamellar microstructure, suitable forging temperatures, and post-forging annealing
chosen.why: Refining the lamellar microstructure through moderate forging and controlled annealing improves both strength (via grain boundary and interface strengthening) and ductility (by promoting uniform deformation and preventing early failure). This is a standard and direct approach in metallurgy to enhance mechanical properties in two-phase alloys.
